people.notes: Chandra Deva (also Soma), the radiant deva of the moon and of the soma nectar; progenitor and eponym of the Chandravamsha, the lunar dynasty from which both the Kurus and the Yadavas descend.
Budha Deva, the deva of the planet Mercury and son of Chandra; husband of Ila.

Son of Budha and Ila; first emperor of the lunar line, famed for his love of the apsara Urvashi. She agreed to live with him on three conditions — never to be seen naked by him, and her two pet rams never harmed — and the Gandharvas broke the compact for her by stealing the rams in the dark, so that he leapt up unclothed by lightning-flash to chase them off; she vanished at once, and he wandered mad with grief until the Gandharvas, moved by it, let them meet again, an evening at a time, and Ayus was born of those nights.
Son of Pururavas and Urvashi.

Son of Ayus; so mighty he briefly took Indra's throne, then fell for his pride and became a serpent. Made regent-Indra while the real Indra hid from the sin of killing the brahmin Vritra; grew so arrogant on the throne he had the seven sages carry his palanquin, and kicked the slow sage Agastya in his impatience, who cursed him to fall to earth as a python. Lived on as a giant serpent, caught and questioned Bhima in its coils during the exile, and was freed of the curse when Yudhishthira answered its riddles.

Son of Nahusha; a great emperor cursed with old age, which his youngest son Puru bore for him. His five sons founded five peoples. Cursed by his father-in-law Shukracharya for taking a second wife, Sharmishtha, behind his first wife Devayani's back; exchanged the curse's old age for a thousand years of his son Puru's youth, exhausted every pleasure without satisfaction, and returned it, naming Puru his heir over his elder sons for the sacrifice. Fell from heaven later for pride, and was carried back up on the merit his grandsons through Madhavi gave him.
Child of Vaivasvata Manu. Lived alternately as the woman Ila (mother of Pururavas by Budha) and the man Sudyumna, whose reign gave the sons below.

The apsara beloved of Pururavas and mother of Ayus. Bound to him only by the condition that he never see her unclothed and her two pet rams go unharmed; lost him for it when the Gandharvas, to end their affair, stole the rams by night and he leapt up by lightning to save them, breaking the condition; relented afterward to grant him one night a year, which is where their sons were born. In an older frame she is also cursed to live a mortal's life on earth for a time, of which Pururavas is that sentence.

First wife of Yayati; daughter of Shukracharya, preceptor of the asuras. Mother of Yadu and Turvasu. Loved Kacha, sent by the devas to learn Shukracharya's death-reviving mantra, and cursed his knowledge useless to him when he refused to marry a guru's daughter; pulled from a dry well by Yayati after Sharmishtha, her own attendant since a childhood quarrel, pushed her in; married Yayati on her father's insistence, on condition Sharmishtha never share his bed — a condition Yayati broke in secret, which is what drew Shukracharya's curse of old age down on him.

Second wife of Yayati; daughter of the asura king Vrishaparva. Mother of Druhyu, Anu and Puru. Made Devayani's handmaiden after pushing her into a well in a childhood quarrel over a garment; asked for Devayani as her own attendant instead as a face-saving condition of her father's surrender; secretly became Yayati's lover and bore him three sons under Devayani's own roof, discovery of which brought Shukracharya's curse down on the king.
Eldest son of Yayati and Devayani; progenitor of the Yadavas (the Yadu line), into which Krishna is born.
Son of Yayati and Devayani; ancestor of the Yavana peoples.
Son of Yayati and Sharmishtha; ancestor of the Bhoja peoples.
Son of Yayati and Sharmishtha; ancestor of the Mleccha peoples.
Youngest son of Yayati and Sharmishtha; he gave his own youth to his aged father and so inherited the throne, founding the Paurava (Kuru) line.
A Paurava emperor descended from Puru through several generations; husband of Shakuntala and father of Bharata.
Daughter of the sage Vishvamitra and the apsara Menaka, raised by the sage Kanva; wife of Dushyanta and mother of Bharata.

The great emperor son of Dushyanta and Shakuntala, after whom the land Bharatavarsha and the Bharata clan are named. Tested as a boy at Kanva's ashram playing fearlessly with lion cubs, counting their teeth; recognised by Dushyanta only after the king's ring, lost and found in a fish, restored his memory of Shakuntala; passed over his own sons for the throne and adopted the sage Bharadvaja's son Vitatha instead, since none of his own were found worthy.
Son of Brihatkshatra; he built Hastinapura, which carries his name. SB 9.21.21

King some generations after Hastin; eponymous ancestor of the Kurus and of the field of Kurukshetra. Ploughed the field himself and sowed it with grains of penance rather than corn, at Indra's asking, to make it forever a ground where any who died fighting or in austerity there would reach heaven — the reason the war his own descendants fought is staged exactly there.
Son of Yadu; the Yadava kings descend from him.
A Yadava king, son of Kroshtu.
A Yadava king of the early Yadu line.
A Yadava king of the early Yadu line.
A Yadava king; progenitor of the Madhava branch, whence Krishna's epithet Madhava. Several generations separate him from Vrishni.
Son of Satvata, and the Vrishni for whom the clan of Krishna is named. SB 9.24.6-12
King of the Kuru line; husband of Sunanda.
Wife of Pratipa; a princess of Shibi and mother of Devapi, Bahlika and Shantanu.

Eldest son of Pratipa; a skin ailment led him to renounce the throne and take to the forest, which is why the throne passed to his younger brother Shantanu instead. Held by tradition to be alive still, a chiranjivi in the hidden village of Kalapa alongside the Ikshvaku king Maru, and expected to return and revive both the solar and lunar lines when the Kali age ends.

Son of Pratipa; ruled the Bahlika kingdom. His descendants fought on the Kaurava side; an elder at the Kuru court through the whole epic, present at the dice game and every council, too bound by kinship to Duryodhana to leave despite disapproving of the war, and killed at Kurukshetra by Bhima on the seventeenth day.

Youngest son of Pratipa; became king when Devapi renounced. Father of Bhishma. Married Ganga on the condition he never question her, and lost her when he broke it over the drowning of their eighth son; years later fell for the fisherman's daughter Satyavati, whose father would only give her if her sons inherited the throne — the demand that made Bhishma take his vow of celibacy.
Son of Bahlika.
Son of Somadatta; a mighty Kaurava warrior slain by Satyaki at Kurukshetra.

The devi of the sacred river; Shantanu's first wife and mother of Bhishma, whom she bore as the last of the eight Vasus made mortal. Drowned her first seven infant sons at birth to return the cursed Vasus to heaven at once, and left Shantanu, as she had warned she would, the moment he broke his vow of never questioning her and asked why she drowned the eighth — sparing Bhishma, and raising him herself before returning him to his father.

Born Devavrata; took a vow of lifelong celibacy so his father could marry Satyavati, hence 'Bhishma'. He was Prabhasa, the eighth and last of the eight Vasus, cursed to a long mortal life for stealing the sage Vasishtha's cow; his seven brother-Vasus, shown here as Ganga's other sons, she returned at once to heaven. Grandsire and regent of the Kurus; a chiranjivi who chose his own hour of death. By name — abducting Amba, Ambika and Ambalika at their swayamvara for Vichitravirya, releasing Amba when she loved another, her vow of revenge and rebirth as Shikhandi, ten days commanding the Kaurava host at Kurukshetra, falling pierced by Arjuna's arrows through Shikhandi shielding him, lying on that bed of arrows through the rest of the war, and teaching Yudhishthira statecraft from it before choosing to die at the sun's turn north (uttarayana).
A Vasu, deva of the earth; a brother-Vasu of Bhishma (Prabhasa), borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the pole star; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the moon; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the day and the ethereal space; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the wind; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of fire (Agni); borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.
A Vasu, deva of the dawn; borne by Ganga and returned to heaven.

A fisherman's daughter, raised by the ferryman Dasharaja; queen of Shantanu and matriarch of the later Kuru line. Before her marriage bore Vyasa to the sage Parashara on an island in the Yamuna, her virginity restored by his boon; her father's condition that only her own sons inherit the throne is what drove Bhishma to his vow; after both her sons Chitrangada and Vichitravirya died without surviving the line properly, she called Vyasa back to father Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura on their widows by niyoga.
A great sage; father of Vyasa by Satyavati before her marriage to Shantanu.

Born to Satyavati by Parashara on an island in the Yamuna, hence Krishna Dvaipayana. He divided the one Veda into four because the age had grown too dull to hold it whole, fathered Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura by niyoga, and composed the epic his own descendants are the cast of. The seventeenth of the avatars, SB 1.3.21. By name — compiling the eighteen Puranas and the Brahma Sutras, dictating the Mahabharata to Ganesha on condition the god never pause for an unintelligible verse, appearing at need throughout the epic to guide his line (granting Sanjaya far-sight to narrate the war, consoling Dhritarashtra, giving Gandhari the vision of her dead sons one last night), and, in the Bhagavata's own frame, the guru who taught it entire to his son Shukadeva.

Elder son of Shantanu and Satyavati; a proud king slain young by a gandharva, leaving no heir. Killed in single combat by a gandharva of the very same name, who considered himself the only rightful bearer of it; his death, without a son, is what put Vichitravirya and then the niyoga line on the Kuru throne instead.

Younger son of Shantanu and Satyavati; wed Ambika and Ambalika but died childless, prompting the niyoga that continued the line. Both wives were won for him by Bhishma at their own swayamvara, abducted from the assembled kings of Kashi; Vichitravirya himself took no part in winning them, and died of consumption within a few years of the marriage, worn out, without an heir.
King of Kashi; his three daughters were carried off from their svayamvara by Bhishma as brides for Vichitravirya.

Eldest Kashi princess; rejected because she loved another, she vowed vengeance on Bhishma and was reborn in Panchala as Shikhandi. Abducted by Bhishma at her sisters' swayamvara for his half-brother Vichitravirya, then sent back on confessing she loved King Shalva; refused by Shalva in turn for having been 'won' by another man, she begged every warrior including Parashurama himself to kill Bhishma, and when none could, took her own life vowing to return as the instrument of his death.
Kashi princess wed to Vichitravirya; mother, through Vyasa's niyoga, of Dhritarashtra, she shut her eyes, so her son was born blind.
Kashi princess wed to Vichitravirya; mother, through Vyasa's niyoga, of Pandu, she paled at the sight of Vyasa, so her son was born pale.
A maidservant of the Kuru queens; mother of Vidura through Vyasa's niyoga.

Born blind to Ambika through Vyasa's niyoga; the elder prince, kept from the throne by his blindness. Father of the Kauravas. By name — his blind favouritism toward Duryodhana through every wrong, from the lac-house to the dice game to the war itself; crushing an iron statue of Bhima to pieces after the war, meant for the real man, on Krishna's warning; and retiring to the forest with Gandhari and Kunti in his last years, dying with them in a forest fire.

Born pale to Ambalika through Vyasa's niyoga; king of Hastinapura. Shot the sage Kindama and his wife while they were coupling in the form of deer, not knowing them for sages, and was cursed to die the instant he embraced a wife in desire — so his five sons were begotten on Kunti's and Madri's mantras by the devas instead. Died breaking that vow at last with Madri, who followed him onto the pyre.

Born to the maid Parishrami through Vyasa's niyoga; an incarnation of Dharma, wisest counsellor of the Kurus, never king by birth of a servant. By name — the Vidura-niti, his counsel to Dhritarashtra against the dice game and the war, ignored every time; warning Yudhishthira of the lac-house plot in riddles the Pandavas alone understood; and retiring at the very end to the forest, where he is said to have poured his own life into Yudhishthira at their last meeting before dying.
Wife of Vidura.
King of Gandhara; father of Gandhari and Shakuni.

Princess of Gandhara; on marrying the blind Dhritarashtra she bound her own eyes for life. By a boon she bore a hundred sons and a daughter. Struck a single mass of flesh from a two-year pregnancy in her grief at Kunti bearing a son first, which Vyasa divided into a hundred and one jars to grow into Duryodhana and his brothers and one sister; cursed Krishna after the war, for letting it happen when he could have stopped it, that his own Yadava line would destroy itself the same way — the curse the Prabhasa killings fulfil.

Prince of Gandhara, Gandhari's brother; master of the loaded dice, he engineered the Kauravas' schemes against the Pandavas. In one telling, Bhishma imprisoned and starved King Subala's whole line for a slight, leaving only Shakuni alive on his dying father's order to avenge them all; the dice he played with at Hastinapura were said to be carved from his own father's bones and obeyed his will. Present at every plot against the Pandavas from the dice game onward; killed at Kurukshetra by Sahadeva.
Son of Shakuni; the Kauravas' envoy to the Pandava camp.

Eldest of the hundred Kauravas; the crown prince whose enmity for the Pandavas drove the war. At his birth jackals howled, an omen he should be cast out. By name — the lac-house at Varanavata built to burn the Pandavas alive, the rigged dice game that won Yudhishthira's kingdom and Draupadi, her disrobing in the Kuru hall that Krishna alone answered, refusing even five villages to avoid war, crowning Karna king of Anga against his own house's objections, eighteen days directing the Kaurava host after Bhishma, Drona and Karna each fell, and dying on the war's last day with his thigh broken by Bhima's mace, the blow Bhima had sworn at the dice game.
Second Kaurava; dragged Draupadi into the assembly and tried to disrobe her, an outrage Bhima avenged by tearing open his breast.

Daughter of Duryodhana; carried off by Krishna's son Samba, which nearly sparked a war.
Son of Duryodhana (Lakshmana Kumara); slain by Abhimanyu inside the chakravyuha.

King of Sindhu, husband of Dushala; his blocking of the Pandavas at the pass sealed Abhimanyu's death, and Arjuna vowed and took his head the next day. Years earlier had tried to abduct Draupadi from the Pandavas' forest hermitage and been captured and humiliated, not killed, by Bhima at Yudhishthira's word; on the thirteenth day of the war held the gate alone against every other Pandava while Abhimanyu broke in and died trapped inside; Arjuna's sunset vow to kill him or immolate himself was fulfilled by Krishna's trick of blotting out the sun so Jayadratha showed himself too soon.
Son of Jayadratha and Dushala.

Eldest Pandava, begotten of Kunti by Dharma (Yama); the just king, never known to lie. By name — winning Draupadi's hand for all five brothers by his mother's unwitting word, founding Indraprastha, the Rajasuya that provoked Duryodhana's envy, losing the kingdom, his brothers, Draupadi and himself at dice, thirteen years' exile including one incognito as Kanka in Virata's court, answering the Yaksha's riddles at the lake to revive his brothers, king again after the war, the Ashvamedha that followed, and at the very end walking to heaven with a dog who was Dharma himself, refusing to abandon it at the gate.

Second Pandava, begotten of Kunti by Vayu; of superhuman strength, sworn to kill all hundred Kauravas. By name — killing the rakshasa Bakasura to free a village, marrying the rakshasi Hidimba and fathering Ghatotkacha, surviving Duryodhana's poisoning and a river-drowning to gain a naga boon of tenfold strength, killing Kichaka in Virata's court for molesting Draupadi, drinking Dushasana's blood at Kurukshetra as sworn over Draupadi's disrobing, and ending the war breaking Duryodhana's thigh in their mace duel.

Third Pandava, begotten of Kunti by Indra; the supreme archer, friend of Krishna, hearer of the Bhagavad Gita. By name — winning Draupadi at her svayamvara by the fish-eye shot, the pilgrimage-exile and marriages to Chitrangada and Ulupi, burning Khandava forest beside Krishna and meeting Agni and Mayasura there, winning Subhadra, the year as Brihannala in Virata's court, penance on Himavat for the Pashupata from Shiva and weapons from the other lokapalas, charioteer scene and the Gita at Kurukshetra, killing Bhishma from behind Shikhandi, Jayadratha within a day as sworn, Karna at last, the post-war Ashvamedha campaign, and the Mahaprasthana into the Himalayas at the end with his brothers.
Fourth Pandava, twin son of Madri by the Ashvins; matchless horseman and the handsomest of men.
Youngest Pandava, twin son of Madri by the Ashvins; wisest of the brothers and a knower of the future.

Kunti's firstborn, begotten by Surya the sun-god before her marriage; set adrift on the river and raised by the charioteer Adhiratha, so his birth lineage stayed unknown even to him. Half-brother of the Pandavas, he fought and died for Duryodhana, learning his kin too late. By name — humiliated at the tournament for his low birth until Duryodhana crowned him king of Anga on the spot, giving away his own protective earrings and armour to Indra in disguise rather than refuse a beggar, Parashurama's curse that his learning would fail him when he needed it most (for lying about his birth to get it), Kunti's night visit before the war asking him to spare his brothers, his promise to spare all but Arjuna, and his death to Arjuna's arrow while his chariot wheel was stuck in the mud and his weapons-knowledge had failed him exactly as cursed.
Son of Satkarma, of the Anga line, and a suta by office. Playing on the bank of the Ganga he found a basket with a child in it, and having no son of his own he raised him: Karna. SB 9.23.12-13
Wife of Adhiratha; foster-mother of Karna, whence his name Radheya.
Wife of Karna.
Son of Karna; a warrior slain by Arjuna at Kurukshetra.
Youngest son of Karna and the only one to outlive the war; taken in and cherished by the Pandavas once his parentage was known.
Son of Yudhishthira and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
Son of Bhima and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
Son of Arjuna and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
Son of Nakula and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
Son of Sahadeva and Draupadi; one of the Upapandavas.
A rakshasi of the forest who loved Bhima during the Pandavas' exile; mother of Ghatotkacha.
Son of Bhima and Hidimba; a rakshasa prince of great sorcery who grew to manhood in a day and died turning the tide of the war, drawing Karna's infallible weapon onto himself.
Wife of Ghatotkacha; mother of Barbarika.

Son of Ghatotkacha; the archer of the three arrows who vowed to fight for whichever side was losing and so gave up his head to Krishna. Came to Kurukshetra with a bow that needed only three arrows to end any war — one to mark every target, one to mark himself, one to finish it; Krishna, seeing he would keep his vow to the losing side over and over and so make the war endless, begged his head as alms before the fighting began; set on a hill, the head watched the whole eighteen days and, asked afterward who really won, said only that it saw Krishna's chakra everywhere the fighting was.
Son of Arjuna and Subhadra; the boy warrior who broke into the chakravyuha and was killed within it, leaving Uttara pregnant with the Kuru line's sole heir.
A Naga princess who wed Arjuna during his wanderings; mother of Iravan and, later, protector of the reborn Arjuna.
Son of Arjuna and Ulupi; raised among the Nagas, he offered himself in sacrifice for the Pandava victory.
Princess of Manipura who wed Arjuna on the condition that their son remain to rule her land; mother of Babhruvahana.
Son of Arjuna and Chitrangada; king of Manipura. Not knowing his father, he met and slew Arjuna in battle during the horse sacrifice; Ulupi's gem restored him to life.
Son of Abhimanyu and Uttara; stillborn but revived by Krishna, he became the sole surviving heir and king of the Kurus after the war.
A princess of Madra; wife of Parikshit and mother of Janamejaya.

Son of Parikshit; the king at whose serpent sacrifice the Mahabharata was first recited, by Vaishampayana, Vyasa's own disciple. Began the sacrifice to avenge his father's death by Takshaka's bite, and kept it burning until Astika, kin to both the sacrificer's court and the nagas being fed into the fire, won a boon before Janamejaya knew what he was granting and made him stop with Vasuki, Takshaka and the rest of the naga race still unburned.
Son of Janamejaya (not to be confused with the Upapandava of the same name); he carried the Kuru throne into the age after the war.
Son of Shatanika; a later Kuru king. The Puranas run the line on through several more kings to Kshemaka, its last.
King of Madra; father of Shalya and Madri.

King of Madra, brother of Madri; a peerless charioteer tricked into fighting for Duryodhana, whom he served as Karna's charioteer. Marching to join the Pandavas, was waylaid with lavish hospitality by disguised Duryodhana's men and, bound by a promise of gratitude given before he knew who had given it, forced to fight for the Kauravas instead; drove Karna's chariot needling him with doubt through his last battle, then took command of the whole army after Karna fell and was killed by Yudhishthira himself, the one Kaurava commander the eldest Pandava faced in person.
Princess of Madra; second wife of Pandu and mother, by the Ashvins, of the twins Nakula and Sahadeva. She followed Pandu onto his pyre.
King of Panchala; father of Drupada.
King of Panchala; humiliated by his old classmate Drona, he won from a sacrifice a son to slay Drona and a daughter to wed the Pandavas.
Child of Drupada, the reincarnation of Amba; born a girl and later made a man, whose presence let Bhishma be brought down, for Bhishma would not fight one born a woman.
Son of Drupada, born from the sacrificial fire; commander of the Pandava army, fated to and did slay Drona.

Also Krishnaa and Yajnaseni; born of the sacrificial fire beside Dhrishtadyumna. Won by Arjuna, she became the shared wife of all five Pandavas and empress of Indraprastha. By name — humiliated and disrobed in the Kuru hall after the dice game, saved when Krishna made her sari endless; her vow not to bind her hair again till washed in Dushasana's blood; disguised as the maid Sairandhri in Virata's court, where she engineered Kichaka's death; and her sons by all five Pandavas (the Upapandavas), killed in their sleep by Ashvatthama after the war.

King of Matsya, in whose court the Pandavas passed their thirteenth year of exile in disguise — Yudhishthira as the courtier Kanka, Bhima the cook Ballava, Arjuna the dance teacher Brihannala, Nakula and Sahadeva as grooms, Draupadi as the queen's maid Sairandhri. Sheltered them through the Kichaka affair and a Kaurava cattle-raid Arjuna alone repelled while still in disguise; gave his daughter Uttara to Abhimanyu once the Pandavas revealed themselves.

Queen of Virata. Took Draupadi, disguised as the maid Sairandhri, into her own service during the Pandavas' year incognito, and sent her to her brother Kichaka's house on an errand not knowing it would end in his death at Bhima's hands for molesting her.
Prince of Matsya (Uttara-kumara / Bhuminjaya); he rode out with the disguised Arjuna against the Kuru cattle-raid.
Princess of Matsya; wed to Abhimanyu and, widowed in the war, mother of Parikshit who carried on the Kuru line.
A Yadava patriarch; father of Devaka and Ugrasena.
Yadava prince, son of Ahuka; father of Devaki.

Yadava king of Mathura, son of Ahuka; deposed by his son Kamsa and restored by Krishna. Kept a virtual prisoner through Kamsa's whole reign of terror; on Kamsa's death Krishna put him back on the throne and himself accepted no kingdom in Mathura, the reason Yadava rule there sits with Ugrasena's house rather than Vasudeva's own.

Son of Ugrasena; the tyrant of Mathura who jailed Devaki and Vasudeva and was slain by the young Krishna. A voice at Devaki's wedding warned that her eighth child would kill him; he killed her first six infants for it and would have killed the seventh (Balarama, moved to Rohini's womb) and eighth (Krishna, smuggled to Gokula) in turn. Sent Putana, Trinavarta, Vatsasura and a train of other demons to kill the boy at Gokula, all failed; finally summoned Krishna and Balarama to a wrestling exhibition at Mathura meaning to have them killed in the ring, and was pulled from his own throne and killed by Krishna before the assembly instead.
Daughter of Devaka, wife of Vasudeva and mother of Krishna; her first sons were killed by her cousin Kamsa.

Shura, son of Vidhuratha of the Vrishni house; ten sons, of whom Vasudeva was the chief, and five daughters, one of them Pritha whom he gave to his friend Kunti. The Bhagavata runs his descent through Chitraratha and Vidhuratha, this tree through Vrishni, and both are recorded. SB 9.24.26-28
Son of Shurasena; father of Krishna, Balarama and Subhadra. Imprisoned by Kamsa, he bore the newborn Krishna across the river to safety.

Also Pritha, daughter of Shurasena, given in fosterage to Kuntibhoja. By name — a mantra from Durvasa that could call any deva to father a child, tested once in girlhood to bear and abandon Karna, then used three times as Pandu's wife to bear Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna (and lent to Madri for Nakula and Sahadeva), Pandu's death beside Madri and her return to Hastinapura with the five boys, surviving Duryodhana's plots at their side, her secret night meeting with Karna before Kurukshetra, and her last years in the forest with Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, dying with them in the fire.
Daughter of Shurasena, sister of Vasudeva; wed to Damaghosha of Chedi and mother of Shishupala.
A childless Bhoja king, cousin of Shurasena; he adopted Pritha, who took his name as Kunti.
Senior wife of Vasudeva; mother of Balarama and Subhadra.

Eighth son of Vasudeva and Devaki, carried across the Yamuna the night he was born and raised by Nanda and Yashoda in Gokula. Of the whole list the Bhagavata sets him apart: krsnas tu bhagavan svayam, the others are portions and portions of portions, and he is the source Himself. The twentieth of the avatars, SB 1.3.23, 1.3.28. Too much story for one note; by name only — Putana, Trinavarta, Shakatasura, Yamalarjuna, Kaliya-damana, the Govardhana lift, the rasa-lila, Akrura's arrival, the Kamsa-vadha, the move to Dvaraka, Rukmini-harana, Jarasandha's seventeen sieges, the Syamantaka jewel, Narakasura-vadha and the sixteen thousand rescued, Shishupala-vadha at Yudhishthira's Rajasuya, Usha-Aniruddha and the war with Bana and Shiva, charioteer at Kurukshetra and speaker of the Bhagavad Gita, Sudama's visit, the Yadava civil war at Prabhasa, and his own end by the hunter Jara's arrow, mistaking his foot for a deer's eye.

Elder brother of Krishna, carried from Devaki's womb into Rohini's, and counted with him as the nineteenth and twentieth descents, born in the house of Vrishni to take the burden off the earth. He carried the plough and the pestle, taught both Duryodhana and Bhima the mace, and would take neither side in the war. The nineteenth of the avatars, SB 1.3.23.
Sister of Krishna, daughter of Rohini; she eloped with Arjuna at Krishna's urging and became the mother of Abhimanyu.
Princess of Vidarbha, sister of Rukmi; chief queen (patrani) of Krishna, held to be an incarnation of Lakshmi.
Daughter of Satrajit; the fiery queen who rode into battle beside Krishna against the demon Narakasura.
Daughter of the bear-king Jambavan; won when Krishna wrestled Jambavan for the Syamantaka gem. Mother of Samba.
The river Yamuna personified; she wed Krishna after long penance on its banks.
An Avanti princess and Krishna's cousin, whom he carried off from her svayamvara.
Princess of Kosala (also called Satya), won by Krishna when he subdued her father's seven fierce bulls.
A Kekaya princess and Krishna's cousin, given to him by her brothers.
A princess of Madra, won by Krishna at her svayamvara.
Son of Krishna and Rukmini; a rebirth of Kamadeva, the god of love.
Son of Krishna and Jambavati; his prank on the sages drew the curse that destroyed the Yadava race.
Daughter of Rukmi; wife of Pradyumna.
Son of Pradyumna; carried off by Usha, daughter of the asura Bana, and rescued by Krishna.
Daughter of the asura Banasura; she wed Aniruddha.
Great-grandson of Krishna; after the Yadavas destroyed themselves he was made their king, so the line survived.
Daughter of King Raivata; born in an earlier age, she was shrunk to human height to become Balarama's wife.

King of Chedi; husband of Shrutashrava and father of Shishupala. His son's death was foretold at birth — a third eye and four arms that would vanish, and his killer named, the moment the boy sat on a particular lap; Krishna's was the lap, and Shishupala's murder-death both took the extra limbs away and, a hundred insults later, ended him at Krishna's hand.
King of Chedi, cousin of Krishna; born three-eyed and four-armed under a doom that Krishna would kill him, which came to pass at Yudhishthira's rajasuya after his hundredth insult.
A great sage; Drona was born of his seed kept in a vessel (drona).

Preceptor in arms to both Kaurava and Pandava princes; brahmin by birth, warrior by trade, commander of the Kaurava host after Bhishma. By name — poverty driving him to Drupada, once his boyhood friend, for help, and Drupada's refusal that made them enemies; teaching the princes at Hastinapura and taking Ekalavya's thumb as fee to keep Arjuna unrivalled; capturing Drupada in return as a training exercise and being given half his kingdom, the seed of Drupada's revenge-son Dhrishtadyumna; eighteen days commanding the Kaurava army at Kurukshetra; and laying down his weapons in grief, believing the false news that his son Ashvatthama was dead, when Dhrishtadyumna beheaded him.
A sage of the Gautama line; father of the twins Kripa and Kripi, born in a clump of reeds and raised in the Kuru court.

Twin of Kripi; a chiranjivi and early teacher of the Kuru princes, he survived the war. Found with his sister as infants in a clump of reeds, born of the sage Sharadvan's seed spilled at the sight of the apsara Janapadi, raised by King Shantanu; one of the four survivors on the Kaurava side after Kurukshetra, and later Parikshit's own teacher.

Twin of Kripa; wife of Drona and mother of Ashwatthama. Found with her brother as infants in a clump of reeds (shara-stamba), born of the sage Sharadvan's seed spilled at the sight of the apsara Janapadi, and raised by King Shantanu.

Son of Drona and Kripi, born with a gem in his brow; a chiranjivi cursed to wander after he slew the Pandava sons in their sleep. Grew up in poverty despite his birth, once tricked as a boy into thinking water was milk; fought the whole war for the Kauravas out of loyalty to his father; on the last night, maddened by Drona's death and appointed commander, crept into the Pandava camp and killed Draupadi's five sons and Dhrishtadyumna in their sleep, mistaking them for the Pandavas themselves; cursed by Krishna, when caught, to wander the earth alone for three thousand years, diseased and friendless, the jewel torn from his forehead.
A king of the Nagas (serpent race); father of Ulupi.
King of Manipura; father of Chitrangada, he gave her to Arjuna on the pledge that their son would inherit his throne.
Son of Drupada; a Panchala warrior who died shielding Yudhishthira in the war.
Son of Balarama and Revati.
Son of Balarama and Revati.
Elder son of Virata; among the first great warriors to fall at Kurukshetra.
Son of Virata, slain early in the war.
A princess of the Shibi people; wife of Yudhishthira.
Son of Yudhishthira and Devika.
A princess of Kashi; wife of Bhima.
Son of Bhima and Balandhara.
A princess of Chedi; wife of Nakula.
Son of Nakula and Karenumati.
A princess won by Sahadeva at her svayamvara; his wife.
Son of Sahadeva and Vijaya.
Son of Shishupala; king of Chedi after his father and an ally of the Pandavas in the war.
Son of Dhrishtadyumna, of the Panchala line.
Son of Shalya of Madra, slain in the war.
Son of Shalya of Madra, slain in the war.
Founder-king of Magadha; father of Jarasandha.
The mighty emperor of Magadha, born in two halves joined by the demoness Jara. Rival of Krishna, he was at last torn apart by Bhima. (A namesake also appears among the hundred Kauravas.)
Daughter of Jarasandha; a queen of Kamsa.
Daughter of Jarasandha; a queen of Kamsa. Kamsa's death at Krishna's hands turned their father into Mathura's implacable enemy.

Son of Bhrigu; guru and reviver of the asuras, keeper of the sanjivani mantra that raises the dead, which Kacha won from him at his own daughter Devayani's insistence. Warned Bali not to grant Vamana's request and was ignored; cursed Devayani's husband Yayati with old age for breaking his word to her over Sharmishtha.
An asura king; father of Sharmishtha.

A king who won brahmarshi-hood by fierce penance; father of Shakuntala by the apsara Menaka. By name — born Kaushika, a kshatriya king who warred with Vasishtha over the wish-cow Nandini and lost, then renounced his throne for penance to become a brahmin's equal; sent Menaka to break that penance, and lost decades of it to her before renewing his resolve; created a rival heaven for Trishanku when the devas refused him; adopted Shunahshepha as Devarata over his own sons' protest; and served finally as Rama's own guru and escort to Mithila, generations after his quarrels with Vasishtha.
An apsara sent to break Vishvamitra's penance; mother of Shakuntala, who was then raised by the sage Kanva.
A Yadava noble, keeper of the Syamantaka gem; father of Satyabhama.
The immortal bear-king of the Ramayan age; Krishna wrestled him for the Syamantaka gem and won his daughter Jambavati.
A thousand-armed asura king and devotee of Shiva; father of Usha.
King Raivata (Kakudmi), who took his daughter Revati to Brahma's realm and returned an age later to a world grown small.
The deva of the sun; an Aditya, son of the devi Aditi and the rishi Kashyap. Father of Karna, whom Kunti bore before her marriage by invoking Surya with a boon she wished to test.
Dharma, the deva of righteousness and lord of justice; father of Yudhishthira, who inherited his unwavering truth.
The deva of the wind; father of the mighty Bhima (and, in the earlier age of the Ramayan, of Hanuman).

King of the devas, wielder of the thunderbolt; an Aditya, son of Aditi and Kashyap, and so a brother of Surya. Father of Arjuna, to whom he later gave celestial weapons and a year's respite from Kurukshetra as Brihannala. By name — killing Vritra with the thunderbolt made from the sage Dadhichi's bones, the many curses on him for seducing Ahalya (a thousand marks that became a thousand eyes, in one telling), losing and regaining his throne across the Bali and Vamana story, and testing Karna by begging his armour and earrings away in disguise.
One of the twin Ashvini Kumaras, devas of dawn and healing; father, by Madri, of Nakula.
One of the twin Ashvini Kumaras, devas of dawn and healing; father, by Madri, of Sahadeva.
Brother of Vasudeva; father of Uddhava.
Brother of Vasudeva, a Vrishni chief.
Brother of Vasudeva, a Vrishni warrior.
Brother of Vasudeva.
Brother of Vasudeva.
Sister of Vasudeva and Kunti; mother of Dantavakra.
Sister of Vasudeva and Kunti; wed to the king of Kekaya.
Sister of Vasudeva and Kunti; mother of Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti.
King of Karusha, son of Shrutadeva; a rebirth of the same doorkeeper of Vishnu as Shishupala, and like him slain by Krishna.
King of Avanti, son of Rajadhidevi; with his brother Anuvinda he fought for the Kauravas (a namesake of one of the hundred Kauravas).
King of Avanti, son of Rajadhidevi and brother of Vinda; a Kaurava ally.
Son of Devabhaga; Krishna's cousin, friend and counsellor, to whom Krishna gave his last teaching.
King of Vidarbha at Kundina; father of Rukmi and of Rukmini.
Prince of Vidarbha, proud brother of Rukmini who opposed her marriage to Krishna; father of Rukmavati.
A Vrishni chief; grandfather of the great warrior Satyaki.
Yuyudhana, grandson of Sini; a mighty Vrishni warrior, pupil of Arjuna and Krishna's charioteer, who fought for the Pandavas.
A Vrishni chief; father of Kritavarma.
Son of Hridika, a Vrishni-Bhoja warrior who fought for the Kauravas and survived the war.

A Yadava elder who bore Krishna and Balarama from Gokula to Mathura; keeper of the Syamantaka jewel for a time. Sent by Kamsa with false honour to fetch the boys to their deaths at the wrestling exhibition, though himself a lifelong devotee overjoyed at the chance to see Krishna, and granted a vision of Vishnu's own form reflected in the Yamuna while bathing on the way; later suspected of hiding the Syamantaka jewel after Prasena's death until its true history with Jambavan came out.
Son of Krishna and Rukmini, a valiant warrior.
Son of Krishna and Satyabhama.
Wife of Nanda; the foster-mother who raised Krishna as her own.
Daughter of Nanda and Yashoda (Ekanamsha); exchanged for the infant Krishna the night he was born.
King of the Nishadas; father of Ekalavya.

Nishada prince who taught himself archery before a clay Drona; Drona claimed his right thumb as guru's fee so none would surpass Arjuna. Practised before the image until he outshot every prince Drona had actually taught, and gave the thumb without a word of protest when asked, crippling his own gift rather than refuse a guru's due; killed years later by Krishna in the Mahabharata's telling, to clear his old debt to Jarasandha's allies before Kurukshetra.
The asura king of Pragjyotisha, son of the earth; Krishna slew him and freed the sixteen thousand women he had imprisoned.
King of Pragjyotisha, son of Narakasura; a Kaurava ally who fought from the great elephant Supratika, slain by Arjuna.
Son of Bhagadatta; king of Pragjyotisha after him.
Charioteer and counsellor of Dhritarashtra, son of the suta Gavalgana; granted divine sight by Vyasa, he narrated the war to the blind king.
Son of Vyasa, born radiant and already renounced; the sage who first recited the Bhagavata.
Wife of Brihaspati, guru of the devas; Chandra bore her away, and of that union was born Budha, sparking the war of the devas and asuras.
Guru of the devas (the planet Jupiter), son of the rishi Angiras; husband of Tara.
A mind-born son of Brahma, one of the Saptarishi and eponym of the Angirasa line; father of Brihaspati.

Son of Brihaspati; sent by the devas to learn from Shukracharya, guru of the asuras, the sanjivani mantra that revives the dead. Killed twice by the asuras for it and twice revived by Shukracharya himself at his daughter Devayani's pleading, until they ground him to ash and mixed it in wine, so that reviving him meant teaching the mantra to what was inside Shukracharya's own body; refused Devayani's love afterward as a guru's son to his guru's daughter, and she cursed his knowledge to fail him — a curse that, since he already taught the devas everything, cost only himself.
Favourite among Chandra's twenty-seven wives, the nakshatras, daughters of Daksha.
Son of Surya Deva; progenitor of humankind in this age and father of Ikshvaku, first of the solar kings.
Son of Vaivasvata Manu; founder of the solar dynasty (Suryavamsha) and first king of Kosala at Ayodhya.

Born from his father Yuvanashva's side. Crying for milk, he was given Indra's own index finger to suck, the deva saying mam ayam dhasyati, he shall suck me: hence Mandhata. Emperor of all seven islands, from where the sun rises to where it sets. Also called Trasaddasyu, because thieves trembled at him. SB 9.6.33-37

The king who kept his word past every ruin. Over him Vishvamitra and Vasishtha quarrelled so long that both were turned into birds and fought on as birds for years. Sonless, he begged a son of Varuna against the promise of sacrificing him. SB 9.7.7-8

Born sa-gara, 'with poison', after his father's co-wife was fed poison while pregnant with him and he survived it. Reformed rather than killed the Yavanas, Shakas, Haihayas and Barbaras who opposed him. His sixty thousand sons by queen Sumati dug the ocean-trench searching for his stolen sacrificial horse, found it beside the meditating sage Kapila, and were burnt to ash in an instant for accusing him of the theft; only Amshuman, son of the other queen Keshini, survived to inherit and later win the horse back peaceably. SB 9.8.5-14
Wayward son of Sagara, exiled for his cruelty.
Grandson of Sagara who recovered the sacrificial horse; father of Bhagiratha.
Son of Amshuman; by fierce penance he brought the Ganga down from heaven to earth to redeem Sagara's sons, hence the river Bhagirathi.
Dilipa II, also Dirghabahu, son of Khatvanga. The ideal king of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha, whose service of the divine cow Nandini won him his son Raghu. SB 9.10.1
Son of Dilipa; so glorious an emperor that the line is called the Raghuvamsha after him.

Son of Raghu; father of Dasharatha. Won Indumati, princess of Vidarbha, at her svayamvara over a hall of rival kings and devas; when a garland dropped by the passing sage Narada's quarrel killed her outright years later, his grief nearly killed him too, restrained only by the sage Vasishtha's counsel that a wise man's grief has a season and a season's end. Raghuvamsha 8.
King of Kosala at Ayodhya; father of Rama by three queens. His promise to Kaikeyi sent Rama into exile and broke his own heart.
Queen of Dilipa, princess of the Magadha line; mother of Raghu.
Princess who chose Aja at her svayamvara; queen of Aja and mother of Dasharatha.
Chief queen of Dasharatha and mother of Rama; a princess of Dakshina Kosala.
Second queen of Dasharatha, princess of Kekaya; her two boons won Bharata the throne and drove Rama to the forest.
Third queen of Dasharatha; mother of the twins Lakshmana and Shatrughna.

Eldest son of Dasharatha and Kausalya of the solar line. The eighteenth of the avatars, SB 1.3.22. By name — Ahalya released from her curse, Vishvamitra's yajna and the killing of Tataka and Subahu, breaking Shiva's bow at Sita's svayamvara, facing down Parashurama on the road home, fourteen years' exile with Sita and Lakshmana, Viradha, Surpanakha turned away and mutilated, Khara and Dushana destroyed, the golden deer Maricha and Sita's abduction, Jatayu's death defending her, alliance with Sugriva and the killing of Vali, Hanuman's leap and the search for Sita, the burning of Lanka, Setubandha, the war and Ravana's death, Sita's agni-pariksha, the coronation at Ayodhya, her later exile on rumour, Lava and Kusha raised at Valmiki's ashram unknowing, Sita's return into the earth, and Rama's own end walking into the Sarayu.
Son of Dasharatha by Kaikeyi; he refused the throne his mother seized and ruled only as regent for Rama's sandals.

Son of Dasharatha by Sumitra; Rama's devoted brother who followed him into exile and warred at his side. By name — fourteen years by Rama and Sita's side unasked, cutting off Surpanakha's nose and ears when she attacked Sita, drawing the Lakshmana-rekha Sita crossed to give alms to the disguised Ravana, wounded near-fatally by Indrajit's shakti weapon and revived by the Sanjeevani herb Hanuman carried whole, and killing Indrajit in the war's last stretch.
Youngest son of Dasharatha by Sumitra, twin of Lakshmana; the slayer of the demon Lavana.
Son of Rama and Sita, born in the forest hermitage; twin of Kusha.
Son of Rama and Sita, born in the forest hermitage; twin of Lava. Kusha and Lava sang the Ramayana before their father, not knowing him.
Son of Lakshmana and Urmila (Lakshmana also had a son Angada, a namesake of the vanara prince).
Son of Bharata and Mandavi; he gave his name to Takshashila.
Son of Bharata and Mandavi.
Son of Shatrughna and Shrutakirti; king of Mathura.
Son of Shatrughna and Shrutakirti.
King of Kekaya; father of Kaikeyi and Yudhajit.
Prince of Kekaya, Kaikeyi's brother, whose invitation took Bharata away from Ayodhya at the hour of Dasharatha's death.
King of Videha; father of Janaka and Kushadhvaja. The Janaka kings descend from Nimi, a son of Ikshvaku.
Siradhvaja, the Janaka of the Ramayana. Ploughing the sacrificial ground he turned up Sita from the furrow, sira, and took her as his daughter. SB 9.13.18-19
Younger brother of Janaka, king of Sankashya.
Queen of Janaka; foster-mother of Sita and mother of Urmila.

Found by Janaka in a furrow of the earth (Bhumija) and raised as his daughter; wife of Rama, carried off by Ravana, at last taken back into the earth. Her birth lineage is none but the Earth's. By name — won at her svayamvara when Rama alone bent and broke Shiva's bow, fourteen years' exile at her own insistence, drawn by the illusion of a golden deer and abducted by Ravana while Rama and Lakshmana were lured away, a year captive in Lanka's Ashoka grove refusing him, found by Hanuman, freed after the war and made to prove her purity by fire (agni-pariksha), exiled again in Ayodhya on a washerman's rumour while pregnant, raising Lava and Kusha alone at Valmiki's ashram, and at their reunion with Rama choosing to return into the earth that bore her rather than prove herself again.
Daughter of Janaka and Sunayana; wife of Lakshmana, who slept fourteen years in her stead so he could guard Rama night and day.
Daughter of Kushadhvaja; wife of Bharata.
Daughter of Kushadhvaja; wife of Shatrughna.
The self-born creator, source of every lineage in this tree: from his mind-born sons spring the devas, the sages, the rakshasas and, through them, the kings of both the solar and the lunar dynasties.
A mind-born son of Brahma (a Prajapati); grandfather of Ravana through his son Vishrava.
Sage son of Pulastya; father of Kubera by Ilavida and of Ravana and his siblings by the rakshasi Kaikasi.
First wife of Vishrava; mother of Kubera.
Rakshasi wife of Vishrava, daughter of the demon Sumali; mother of Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Shurpanakha and Vibhishana.
Son of Vishrava and Ilavida; the yaksha lord of wealth who first ruled Lanka, until his half-brother Ravana drove him out.

The ten-headed rakshasa king of Lanka; a mighty devotee of Shiva and master of the Vedas whose abduction of Sita brought his doom. By name — penance for boons from Brahma (near-invincibility, but not against men or vanaras, which he thought beneath asking), seizing Lanka from his half-brother Kubera and the Pushpaka chariot with it, composing the Shiva Tandava Stotram after Shiva pinned him under Kailasa for trying to lift it, Surpanakha's mutilation drawing him to Panchavati, the golden-deer ruse and Sita's abduction, Jatayu's failed rescue, Vibhishana's defection when he refused to return her, the burning of Lanka by Hanuman, Kumbhakarna and Indrajit dying in the war before him, and his own death to Rama's Brahmastra.
Giant brother of Ravana, cursed to sleep six months at a time; woken for the war, he was slain by Rama.
Sister of Ravana whose courting of Rama and Lakshmana, and the loss of her nose, set the war in motion.
Youngest brother of Ravana; righteous, he deserted to Rama and was crowned king of Lanka after the war.
Mayasura, the great asura architect; father of Mandodari.
Daughter of Mayasura; the wise and virtuous chief queen of Ravana and mother of Indrajit.
Meghanada, son of Ravana and Mandodari; he once defeated Indra himself, hence his name, and was slain by Lakshmana.
Son of Ravana and Mandodari; a colossal warrior slain by Lakshmana.
Young son of Ravana, slain by Hanuman in the burning of Lanka.
Son of Kumbhakarna, killed in the war.
Son of Kumbhakarna, killed in the war.
Wife of Kumbhakarna; a granddaughter of the demon Virochana.
The vanara king of Kishkindha; foster-father of Vali and Sugriva, who were begotten of the gods Indra and Surya.
Elder vanara prince, son of Indra; king of Kishkindha of peerless strength, slain by Rama's arrow to restore Sugriva.
Younger vanara prince, son of Surya; exiled by Vali and restored by Rama, whose army of vanaras he then led to Lanka.
Vanara elder and physician; father of Tara.
Daughter of Sushena; the wise queen of Vali, and after him of Sugriva. Mother of Angada.
Wife of Sugriva. Seized by Vali along with the kingdom when he exiled his brother on a misunderstanding; restored to Sugriva only after Rama killed Vali to keep his alliance's promise.

Son of Vali and Tara; the vanara prince who led Rama's embassy to Ravana. Made yuvaraja by Sugriva out of guilt at having killed his father Vali; led the party that found Sita in Lanka after Hanuman's own search failed elsewhere; and went as Rama's envoy into Ravana's own court to demand Sita's return, planting his foot and daring any rakshasa to move it before the whole assembly, which none could.
A vanara chief; the earthly father of Hanuman.

The apsara Punjikasthala, called Managarva in the Puranic account, cursed into the body of a vanara and born a princess of Kishkindha. She and Kesari propitiated Vayu for a son and got Hanuman. Rama 4.66; Puranic Encyclopaedia, Anjana

Kesari + Anjana (apsara Punjikasthala, cursed); Vayu-begotten. Chiranjivi; Shaiva reading: Rudra-avatar. Leapt to Lanka; found Sita; burned the city with his own tail; carried the whole Sanjeevani mountain, not knowing which herb. Lifelong brahmachari; married Suvarchala, Surya's daughter, as guru-dakshina for the last of the nine grammars — a union Surya himself called for the world's good, not a breach of the vow (Parashara Samhita, not the Bhagavata; a Telangana temple tradition). Rama 1.17, 4.66, 5.1; Shiva Purana 3.20.
A rakshasa lord of the elder line of Lanka; father of Kaikasi, whom he gave to the sage Vishrava to sire sons who might rival the devas.
Son of Kusha; a king of the Raghu line.
A king of Kosala descended from Rama.
Disciple of Jaimini, master of the yoga of the mystics, and the teacher from whom Yajnavalkya received that yoga. SB 9.12.3-4
Perfected in yoga and living still, the Puranas say, in the village of Kalapa. At the end of the age of Kali he will begin the solar dynasty again. SB 9.12.5-6

The last of the solar kings the Purana counts as past: he fought at Kurukshetra on the Kaurava side and was killed by Abhimanyu. He and Abhimanyu therefore stand on the same generation, which is what fixes the war's place in this whole tree. SB 9.12.8-9
Daughter of Dasharatha and Kausalya, elder sister of Rama, given in adoption to King Romapada of Anga; wife of the sage Rishyasringa, whose rite granted Dasharatha his sons.

Citraratha, called Romapada, king of Anga. Sonless, he was given his friend Dasharatha's daughter Shanta as his own, and married her to Rishyasringa; by the sage's grace he got a son at last. SB 9.23.7-10
A sage raised without knowledge of women; his coming ended a drought, and his fire-rite gave Dasharatha his four sons. Husband of Shanta.
Son of Ravana, a fierce warrior slain by the vanara Angada.
Son of Ravana, slain by Hanuman.
Three-headed son of Ravana, slain by Hanuman.
Wife of Indrajit (Meghanada), daughter of the naga king Shesha; on his death she followed him onto the pyre.
An elder rakshasa lord; father of Sumali and Malyavan.
Grand old rakshasa, brother of Sumali; the wise elder who counselled Ravana to return Sita and make peace.
Son of Sumali and maternal uncle of Ravana; chief commander of Lanka's army, slain by the vanara Nila.
Rakshasi wife of Vibhishana; she comforted Sita in captivity.
Daughter of Vibhishana and Sarama; the kind rakshasi who watched over Sita and foretold Rama's victory.
Vanara son of Vishwakarma; the architect who built Rama's bridge across the sea to Lanka.
Vanara chief, son of Agni; a commander of Rama's army.
Charioteer of Surya, elder brother of Garuda; father of the vulture-kings Jatayu and Sampati.
Vulture-king, son of Aruna; he gave his life trying to stop Ravana from carrying Sita away.
Vulture-king, elder brother of Jatayu; his far sight found Sita in Lanka for Rama's searchers.
A mind-born son (Prajapati) of Brahma; father of Kashyap.
A mind-born son of Brahma, one of the Saptarishi; father of Chandra (Soma).
A Prajapati; father of the many wives of Kashyap, and so grandfather of the devas, nagas, birds and much else.
The great progenitor rishi; by his many wives, father of the devas (Adityas), the asuras, the nagas and the birds.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Adityas, the devas.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the sun's charioteer Aruna and of Garuda.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the nagas.
Son of Kashyap and Vinata; the mighty eagle who bears Vishnu.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Daitya asuras.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Danava asuras.

Daitya king, son of Kashyap and Diti; slain by Vishnu as Narasimha for tormenting his devotee son Prahlada. Won from Brahma a boon against death by man or beast, by day or night, indoors or out, on earth or in the sky, by any weapon — and was torn apart on Narasimha's lap, at the threshold of a doorway, at twilight, by claws, on neither ground nor sky. Twin of Hiranyaksha, killed a generation earlier by Varaha.

Daitya, son of Kashyap and Diti; slain by Vishnu as the boar Varaha. Dragged the earth down into the cosmic waters, and was killed in the duel that followed when Varaha lifted her back out on his tusks. Twin of Hiranyakashipu, killed a generation later as Narasimha.

Son of Hiranyakashipu; a supreme devotee of Vishnu whom no torment could shake. By name — surviving poison, elephants, fire, cliffs and serpents at his own father's order for refusing to renounce Vishnu, answering 'everywhere, even in this pillar' when asked where his god was, and Vishnu tearing out of that pillar as Narasimha to kill Hiranyakashipu across a threshold at twilight, neither in nor out, neither day nor night, neither man nor beast — every loophole in the asura's own boon closed at once.
Son of Prahlada; a Daitya king, father of Bali.

Mahabali, son of Virochana; the generous asura emperor whom Vishnu, as the dwarf Vamana, measured out of the three worlds. His line runs on to Banasura of the Mahabharat age (Usha's father). Refused his guru Shukracharya's warning not to grant the dwarf's request; gave anyway when Vishnu's second step took heaven along with earth, and offered his own head for the third when there was nothing left to give, for which Vishnu let him keep Patala and promised him Indra's seat in a future age.
King of the nagas, son of Kashyap and Kadru; the serpent-rope of the ocean's churning.

A naga king, son of Kashyap and Kadru; his bite would one day slay Parikshit. Killed the king in fulfilment of a rishi's curse after Parikshit, hunting, had insulted a silent sage by hanging a dead snake round his neck; hid afterward from Parikshit's son Janamejaya's snake-sacrifice inside Indra's own court, and was saved along with Vasuki and the rest of his kind when Astika stopped the sacrifice at the last moment.
Ananta, the endless serpent, son of Kashyap and Kadru, on whom Vishnu reclines.
Goddess of speech and wisdom, consort of Brahma; mother of his mind-born sons.
A mind-born son of Brahma, a Prajapati and Saptarishi; father of Shukracharya, guru of the asuras.

A mind-born son of Brahma, chief of the Saptarishi and family priest of the Ikshvaku kings; forefather of the line of Parashara and Vyasa. By name — the long rivalry with Vishvamitra, sparked when Vishvamitra coveted his wish-fulfilling cow Nandini/Kamadhenu and was refused; all hundred of his sons killed by Vishvamitra's curse, after which he tried and failed to end his own life by fire, water and cliff, each element refusing to harm him; the Trishanku and Harishchandra quarrels that turned him and Vishvamitra into birds fighting for years; cursing King Saudasa into the rakshasa Kalmashapada, then fathering his heir on Kalmashapada's queen Madayanti by niyoga after the king's death; and a later son, Shakti, father of Parashara and so grandfather of Vyasa.
Son of Vasishtha and father of Parashara; of the Vasishtha line.
Son of Pururavas; founder of the Kanyakubja (Kaushika) branch of the lunar line.

King of the Kaushikas; father of Vishvamitra and of Satyavati, who married the sage Richika and bore Jamadagni. Vishvamitra's own royal birth, before his penance won him brahmin status, runs through Gadhi.
Sanjna, daughter of Vishvakarma and chief wife of Surya; mother of Vaivasvata Manu, Yama, Yami and the Ashvin twins.
The shadow-image of Sandhya, second wife of Surya; mother of Shani, Tapati and Savarni Manu.
Daughter of Surya and Sandhya, twin of Yama; the river-goddess Yamuna.
Son of Surya and Chaya; the slow, stern planet Saturn.
Daughter of Surya and Chaya; wed King Samvarana, an ancestress of the Kurus.
Son of Surya and Chaya; the Manu of a coming age (Savarni Manu).
One of the twenty-seven nakshatras, daughters of Daksha and wives of Chandra.
One of the twenty-seven nakshatras, daughters of Daksha and wives of Chandra.
One of the twenty-seven nakshatras, daughters of Daksha and wives of Chandra.

One of the twenty-seven nakshatras, daughters of Daksha and wives of Chandra.
Wife of Vaivasvata Manu; mother of Ila and of the Manu sons who founded the earth's royal houses.
Son of Manu; his line held Anarta and Kusasthali (Dvaraka's site).

Son of Manu; forebear of a solar branch. In one telling, away at his father's sacrifice when his brothers divided the inheritance without him, he was directed by his father to claim what the priests kept as their fee instead; the Angirasa priests, testing his honesty, gave him everything when he refused to take even that without their leave.
Son of Manu; a king cursed to live as a lizard for a gift gone wrong.
Son of Manu.
Son of Manu; forebear of the Vaishya kings.
Son of Manu, made a shudra for slaying his guru's cow.
A mighty son of Kashyap and Diti, of adamantine body; father, by Varangi, of Tarakasura.
Wife of Vajranga; mother of Tarakasura.
Asura son of Vajranga and Varangi, boon-armoured against all but a son of Shiva; slain at last by Kartikeya. Father of the three lords of Tripura.
Son of Tarakasura; a lord of the flying triple-city Tripura.
Son of Tarakasura; a lord of Tripura.
Son of Tarakasura; a lord of Tripura, the three cities burnt by Shiva.
Foremost of the Danava sons of Kashyap and Danu; wed Simhika and fathered Rahu.
A Danava son of Danu, slain by Indra with sea-foam.
A Danava sorcerer-king, son of Danu; foe of Pradyumna.
Aditya lord of the waters and cosmic order.
Aditya of friendship and contracts, paired with Varuna.
Aditya of custom, patron of marriage and the ancestors.
Aditya of fortune and inherited share.
Aditya of roads, herds and safe journeys.

The dwarf brahmin who came to Bali's sacrifice and asked for three steps of ground, then took the earth with one and the sky with the second, and set the third on Bali's own head. Son of Kashyapa and Aditi, and so a brother of Indra, whose lost heaven he was recovering. The fifteenth of the avatars, SB 1.3.19.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of cattle, the wish-granting cows.
The wish-fulfilling cow, daughter of Surabhi.
Divine cow, daughter of Surabhi, kept by the sage Vasishtha.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the birds of prey.
Daughter of Tamra; mother of hawks and falcons.
Daughter of Tamra; mother of kites and vultures.
Daughter of Tamra; mother of the vultures.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the apsaras.
Foremost of the apsaras, daughter of Muni.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of fierce Danavas.

Asura who held back the world's waters; slain by Indra with the thunderbolt Vajra, made from the bones of the sage Dadhichi, who gave them freely for it. In the Bhagavata's own account he is also, at once, the self-realised king Chitraketu reborn under a curse of Parvati's, so that killing him cost Indra nothing spiritually — the being had no fear of death to begin with.
A Danava son of Danayus.
Daughter of Diti (sister of Hiranyakashipu); wife of Viprachitti, mother of Rahu.
Son of Viprachitti and Simhika; the severed asura-head that swallows sun and moon at eclipses.
A great naga king, son of Kashyap and Kadru.
A naga of Kadru's line (namesake of Indra's elephant).
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Gandharvas.
King of the Gandharvas (Angaraparna); Arjuna bested him on the Ganga and he gave the Pandavas the Chakshushi lore and celestial horses.
A Gandharva master of music, singer in Indra's court.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; a mother of serpents, and the sea-nagi who tested Hanuman's wit on the leap to Lanka.
The hundred-hooded serpent of the Yamuna, quelled when Krishna danced upon his hoods.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the beasts of the wild.
Daughter of Krodhavasha; mother of lions, tigers and the great cats.
Daughter of Krodhavasha; mother of the monkeys and the horses.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of trees, creepers and grasses.
Lord of the forest trees, child of Ira; the standing green world.
King of the Kuru line who wed Tapati, Surya's daughter; father of Kuru, the dynasty's eponym.
Son of Sharyati; his realm Anarta held the coast where Dvaraka would rise.
Son of Bhrigu; the aged sage restored to youth by the Ashvins, husband of Sukanya. The rejuvenating tonic Chyavanprash, which the Ashvins first prepared for him, is named after him.

Daughter of King Sharyati; devoted wife of the sage Chyavana. Struck his eyes by accident as a girl, mistaking them for fireflies in an anthill where he had sat motionless through long penance, and married him at her father's order to atone; when the Ashvin twins offered to make him young and beautiful if she chose correctly between three identical men, she picked her own aged husband by his eyes alone and stayed loyal, and Chyavana in turn taught the Ashvins the Soma sacrifice's own share, over Indra's objection.

Bhargava sage of the fire of wrath, born of the Bhrigu line through Chyavana. His pregnant mother hid her unborn child in her thigh (uru, his name) when kshatriyas bent on wiping out the Bhrigus for their wealth attacked her; born already blazing, his fury at the slaughter of his kin threatened to burn up the three worlds until his ancestors begged him to spend it elsewhere, and he deposited it in the ocean instead, as the submarine fire (vadavagni) that will one day end the age. Gave that same fire-power to Sagara, his descendant, who used it to annihilate the Talajanghas — closing a loop the quarrel that spared the world opened.

A Bhargava sage; husband of Satyavati, Gadhi's daughter, and father of Jamadagni. Prepared two portions of a magic rice-dish, one for his wife to bear a brahmin son and one for her mother to bear a warrior son; the two women swapped bowls, which is why Vishvamitra, Satyavati's own brother, was born a kshatriya who had to win brahminhood by penance, and why Jamadagni's son Parashurama carries kshatriya fire in a brahmin line.
Daughter of King Gadhi and sister of Vishvamitra; wife of Richika.
Bhargava rishi, son of Richika; husband of Renuka, father of Parashurama.
Wife of Jamadagni, mother of Parashurama; a devoted and much-tried queen.

Rama of the axe, called Bhrigupati for his house. He killed Kartavirya Arjuna over the stolen cow and then cleared the earth of kshatriyas twenty-one times, and lived on to teach Bhishma, Drona and Karna, three ages of this tree apart. The sixteenth of the avatars, SB 1.3.20.
Aditya, the divine artificer (Vishvakarma); father of Sanjna (Sandhya), Surya's wife.
Three-headed son of Tvashtar, priest to the devas, beheaded by Indra.
Wife of Atri, a paragon of virtue; mother of Dattatreya, Durvasa and Chandra.

Son of Atri and Anasuya, born because she prayed for an incarnation. He gave the teaching of transcendence to Alarka, to Prahlada and to Kartavirya Arjuna, all three of whom stand in this tree, and the mystic perfections he gave Kartavirya are what made that king unkillable by anyone but Parashurama. The sixth of the avatars, SB 1.3.11.
Son of Atri and Anasuya; the wrath-swift sage whose boon gave Kunti her deva-sons.
Severed body of the eclipse-asura, brother of Rahu; the descending shadow-node.
Asura son of Simhika who, with Ilvala, preyed on guests until the sage Agastya digested him.
Asura son of Simhika; brother of Vatapi.
Wife of Hiranyakashipu, mother of Prahlada; kept safe by Narada while her lord warred with heaven.
Brother of Prahlada, son of Hiranyakashipu.
Brother of Prahlada, son of Hiranyakashipu.
Brother of Prahlada, son of Hiranyakashipu.
Daitya son of Hiranyaksha (or of Shiva's sweat), the blind asura slain by Shiva.
Wife of Bali; queen of the generous asura emperor.
Daughter of Daksha, wife of Kashyap; mother of the Yakshas and Rakshasas.
Progenitor of the yakshas, the guardian nature-spirits of wealth.
Progenitor of the rakshasas, the night-wandering kind.
The pot-born sage, son of Mitra and Varuna; who drank the ocean, humbled the Vindhya, and digested the asura Vatapi. Husband of Lopamudra.
Princess fashioned for the sage Agastya; his learned wife and a hymn-seer in her own right.
Son of Hastin; founder of the Ajamidha branch of the Puru line, from whom Panchala and Kuru both descend. SB 9.21.
Son of Ajamidha; ancestor of the Kuru line.
Son of Kuru; carries the throne onward through Jahnu's branch.
Kuru-line king, descended from Viduratha.
Kuru-line king; not the Parikshit of the Mahabharata's own generation, born generations earlier. Namesake, see PURANIC_LINEAGES.md Part V.
Kuru-line king, father of Pratishravas. Not the Pandava Bhima.
Kuru-line king, descended from Bhimasena.
Son of Puruja, in the Ajamidha-to-Panchala chain. SB 9.21.
Son of Arka; father of five sons who divided the Panchala realm between them — Mudgala, Yavinara, Brihadvishva, Kampilla and Sanjaya. SB 9.21.
Eldest of Bharmyashva's five sons, eponym of the Mudgala gotra; husband of Indrasena (Nalayani, Damayanti's niece — see the Nalopakhyana notes) after her hundred trials of him.
Son of Mudgala; father of Divodasa of Panchala. RV 6.61. The tree keeps this reading against the Bhagavata's alternative, which has Mudgala father Divodasa directly.
King of Panchala; patron of the Rigvedic sage Bharadvaja, father of Mitrayu. RV 1.130, 6.26. Not Divodasa of Kashi — see PURANIC_LINEAGES.md Part V.
Son of Divodasa of Panchala; father of Chyavana of Panchala.
Panchala king, son of Mitrayu. Not the sage Chyavana, Bhrigu's son and Sukanya's husband — see PURANIC_LINEAGES.md Part V.
King of Panchala; the Rigvedic Sudas Paijavana of the Battle of the Ten Kings (dasarajna), with Vasishtha as his priest. RV 7.18, 7.33, 7.83. Not the Ikshvaku Sudasa — see Part V.
Panchala king, son of Sudasa. Not the Pandava Sahadeva.
Panchala king, son of Sahadeva; his line runs down toward Drupada.

Twin of Divodasa in the royal Panchala line; also told as Brahma-born (the divine ray). Famed as the wife of Gautama, cursed and later redeemed.
Gautama Maharishi, of the Angirasa gotra (descended from Utathya, son of Angiras). Husband of Ahalya.
Son of Gautama and Ahalya; purohita of King Janaka of Videha.
Son of Gautama and Ahalya; the son who deliberated so long he spared a rash act (Mahabharata).

King of Nishadha, son of Virasena. Master of horses and of cookery, and beloved of Damayanti before either had seen the other. Possessed by Kali, he gambled his kingdom away to his brother Pushkara, abandoned Damayanti in the forest, and lived disfigured as Bahuka, charioteer and cook to Rituparna of Ayodhya, until the science of horses he traded for the science of dice gave him both back. MBh 3.50-78

Princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhima, who loved Nala on report alone and knew him at her svayamvara among four devas wearing his face, because only his feet touched the ground. Abandoned in the forest, she made her way back by a brahmin's recognition and drew her husband out of hiding with a riddling verse. MBh 3.50-78
Also called Indrasena; daughter of Nala and Damayanti, wife of Mudgala.
Eponym of the Maudgalya gotra: the Brahmin line of Mudgala’s descendants, distinct from the royal Panchala line carried by Vadhryasva.
Somaka’s eldest son; offered in sacrifice, per the Mahabharata, so that Somaka might gain a hundred sons.
Asura brother of Vatapi; the pair who preyed on guests until Agastya digested Vatapi.
Wife of Vasishtha; the star Alcor, paired with him as the archetypal devoted couple.
Also Indrani/Pulomaja; queen of the devas, wife of Indra.
Son of Indra and Shachi.
Daughter of Indra; wed to Shukracharya.

Goddess of wine (sura); rose from the churning of the ocean of milk and was claimed by the asuras. SB 8.8.

Eldest of Ikshvaku's hundred sons. Banished for eating a hare from the sacrificial offering, hence Shashada, the hare-eater; recalled to the throne at his father's death. SB 9.6.6-8
Fought the demons for the devas mounted on Indra, who had taken the form of a bull: seated on its hump he is Kakutstha, and as the vehicle of Indra, Indravaha. SB 9.6.11-15
Son of Puranjaya. SB 9.6.16
Fifth of the solar kings. Not Vena's son Prithu, for whom the earth is named. SB 9.6.16
Son of Vishvagandhi. Not Chandra Deva of the lunar line. SB 9.6.17
Built Shravasti Puri, the city that kept his name. SB 9.6.20
Killed the demon Dhundhu with twenty-one thousand sons at his side, and took the name Dhundhumara, slayer of Dhundhu. All but three of the sons burned in the fire the demon breathed. SB 9.6.21-24
One of the three sons who survived Dhundhu's fire, with Kapilashva and Bhadrashva. SB 9.6.23-24
Son of Haryashva. Not the rakshasa Nikumbha of Lanka. SB 9.6.24

A hundred wives and no son. The sages held an Indra-yajna for him in the forest; thirsty in the night he drank the consecrated water himself, and in time bore the child from his own right side. SB 9.6.25-32

Given Narmada, sister of the Nagas, by her serpent brothers; she carried him down to Rasatala where, empowered by Vishnu, he killed the Gandharvas. Whoever remembers it is safe from snakes. SB 9.7.2-3; RV 6.20.10
Bears his great-grandfather's epithet as his name. In the Rigveda he is called ardhadeva, half-god, a word used of no one else. SB 9.7.4; RV 4.42.8-9

Cursed by his own father into a chandala for carrying off a brahmin's bride at her wedding. Vishvamitra sent him bodily to heaven; the devas threw him back; Vishvamitra stopped him mid-fall, and he hangs there yet, head downward. SB 9.7.5-6

The son promised to Varuna before his birth and deferred past every excuse; he took bow and arrows to the forest to stay alive, and came back six years later having bought Shunahshepha in his place. SB 9.7.9-20
Built Champapuri, which later became the capital of Anga. SB 9.8.1
Driven out by his enemies, he died in the forest. His pregnant widow was poisoned by her co-wives but the child was born alive, carrying the poison: sa-gara. SB 9.8.2-5
Tried to bring the Ganga down to redeem Sagara's sons and died without succeeding. Not the Dilipa of the Raghuvamsha, who is four generations below Khatvanga. SB 9.9.1
Son of Bhagiratha. SB 9.9.16

King of Ayodhya, and the friend of Nala. He gave Nala the akshahridaya, the heart of the dice, and took from him the ashvavidya, the science of horses. Nala served in his kitchen and at his reins under the name Bahuka. SB 9.9.16-17; MBh 3.65-70
Not Sudasa of Panchala, nor the Rigvedic Sudas Paijavana of the Bharatas. SB 9.9.18

Also Mitrasaha. Cursed by Vasishtha into a rakshasa; in that state he devoured a brahmin, and the widow cursed him to die at his next embrace. Twelve years sonless, he let Vasishtha beget his heir on his queen Madayanti. SB 9.9.20-38
Carried for years and finally born when Vasishtha struck his mother's womb with a stone, ashman. SB 9.9.38
Survived Parashurama's purge of the kshatriyas screened by a ring of women, hence Narikavacha, armoured in women; and because the kshatriyas began again from him, Mulaka, the root. SB 9.9.39-40
Son of Balika, and not the father of Rama. SB 9.9.41
Fought at the devas' side and won; offered a boon, he asked only how long he had to live, was told a few moments, left heaven at once and gave those moments entirely to Hari. SB 9.9.41-49
Son of Nishadha. SB 9.12.1
Said to be born of the sun's effulgence. SB 9.12.2
The last king the Raghuvamsha follows. SB 9.12.5
Son of Prasenajit. Not Takshaka the Naga who killed Parikshit. SB 9.12.7

Second son of Ikshvaku. He would not wait for Vasishtha to finish Indra's sacrifice before beginning his own, and the two cursed each other's bodies to fall. From his preserved body, churned by the sages, Janaka was born. SB 9.13.1-11

Born of no womb, from the churning of his father's body: hence Vaideha, the bodiless-born, and Mithi, the churned, and Mithila for the city he founded. Every king of this line is called Janaka after him. SB 9.13.12-13
Not Shunahshepha, whom Vishvamitra adopted under the same name. SB 9.13.14
Not Maru of Kalapa in the Ikshvaku line. SB 9.13.15
A self-realized king; his cousin Khandikya was expert in ritual, and the two exchanged what each lacked. SB 9.13.21-22
Brother of Kritadhvaja. SB 9.13.21
Son of Mitadhvaja, master of ritual, who fled Keshidhvaja and later taught him karma-kanda in exchange for knowledge of the self. SB 9.13.22

Yadava emperor of the world, a great mystic who held fourteen jewels; ten thousand wives and a lakh of sons by each. His daughter Bindumati married Mandhata of the solar line, and their two houses meet in her. SB 9.23.31-32

Daughter of the Yadava emperor Shashabindu; queen of Mandhata, mother of Purukutsa, Ambarisha and Muchukunda and of fifty daughters. The cleanest marriage between the solar and lunar lines in the Puranas. SB 9.6.38
Son of Mandhata, and the most prominent of the three; accepted as son by his own grandfather Yuvanashva. Not Ambarisha the devotee, of Nabhaga's branch, whom Durvasa cursed. SB 9.7.1

Son of Mandhata. He guarded the devas through a war of ages until Kartikeya came to relieve him, and when they offered him any boon but liberation he asked for sleep, and that whoever woke him should burn. He slept in a cave through the ages. Krishna led Kalayavana into that cave; Kalayavana kicked the sleeping man, and was ash before he understood. Then Muchukunda, who had lain down in his father's age, opened his eyes on Vishnu. SB 9.6.38, 10.51
Son of Ambarisha. SB 9.7.1
With Ambarisha and Yauvanashva, one of the three most prominent in Mandhata's line. SB 9.7.1

One of the fifty daughters of Mandhata and Bindumati. The Puranas name none of them individually, so she stands here for all fifty, who chose Saubhari together and then quarrelled over him, each certain he was hers alone. SB 9.6.38-44

Deep in the Yamuna at his austerity he watched a pair of fish mate, and desire took him. He asked Mandhata for a daughter; the king, seeing grey hair and a trembling head, said only that his daughters chose for themselves. So Saubhari made himself young, and all fifty chose him. By his mantras he built each of them a palace, and in his own words: I became the husband of fifty wives, and in each of them I begot one hundred sons, and thus my family increased to five thousand. Then he saw what the fish had cost him, took vanaprastha, and his wives followed him. SB 9.6.39-55
Sister of the Nagas, given to Purukutsa by her serpent brothers at Vasuki's bidding, and the river of that name. SB 9.7.2

A brahmin of Garga's line, mocked as impotent by Syala in the Yadava assembly. He went to the western sea and lived twelve years on iron filings until Shiva granted him a son who would break the Yadavas. HV 58; VP 5.23
The apsara who took the form of a cowherd woman and bore Gargya his son. Called Rambha in some recensions. HV 58

Born of Gargya and the apsara Gopali, and raised by the childless king of the Yavanas. Narada pointed him at Mathura and he came with thirty million soldiers. Krishna, carrying no weapon, ran from him into a mountain cave, where Kalayavana kicked a sleeping man he took for Krishna, and Muchukunda's first waking glance burned him to ash. SB 10.50-51
The childless king of the Yavanas, Gargya's friend, who raised Kalayavana as his own. VP 5.23
A starving brahmin who sold his middle son to be Harishchandra's sacrifice, and took a further fee to hold the knife himself. SB 9.7.20; AB 7.13-16

Bought by Rohita to die in his place, he praised the devas from the stake until his bonds fell away. Vishvamitra adopted him as Devarata, god-given, over the protests of his own sons. His brothers were Shunahpuccha and Shunolangula. SB 9.7.20-26; AB 7.13-18
Eldest son of Ajigarta, whom his father would not sell. AB 7.15
Youngest son of Ajigarta, whom his mother would not give. AB 7.15
Son of Puru. Not Parikshit's son. SB 9.20.1
Ten sons by the apsara Ghritachi: Riteyu, Kaksheyu, Sthandileyu, Kriteyuka, Jaleyu, Sannateyu, Dharmeyu, Satyeyu, Vrateyu and Vaneyu. SB 9.20.3-4
Eldest of Raudrashva's ten. SB 9.20.5
Three sons: Sumati, Dhruva and Apratiratha, whose son Kanva raised Shakuntala. SB 9.20.6
Son of Rantinava. SB 9.20.6

Son of Apratiratha, kshatriya-born and a brahmin by life. He found the infant Shakuntala in the forest where Menaka had left her, brought her to his ashram and raised her; it was under his roof that Dushyanta met her. SB 9.20.6-11
Son of Kanva; his sons, headed by Praskanna, were all brahmins. SB 9.20.7

Bharata's sacrifices gave him no worthy heir, and Bharadvaja, the son Brihaspati begot on Mamata, was given to him instead: given away he is Vitatha, the one who was otherwise. The same sage appears in this tree in his own right, in the Angirasa line, as the father of Drona. SB 9.20.37-38
Five sons: Brihatkshatra, Jaya, Mahavirya, Nara and Garga. SB 9.21.19
Eldest of Manyu's five. SB 9.21.19, 9.21.21
Son of Manyu. SB 9.21.19
Son of Nara; father of Guru and of Rantideva. SB 9.21.1

He gave away his own food until he and his household fasted. Emperor of all seven islands, who received the eight mystic perfections from Dattatreya and ruled eighty-five thousand years with his strength and memory unbroken. He took Jamadagni's cow, and Parashurama killed him for it, and then killed the kshatriyas twenty-one times over. Of his thousand sons five survived. SB 9.23.24-27

Sonless, and too afraid of his barren queen Shaibya to take another wife. The devas made the words true: Shaibya bore Vidarbha, and Vidarbha grew up and married the girl. SB 9.23.34-38
Born to Jyamagha and Shaibya by the mercy of the devas; three sons, Kusha, Kratha and Romapada. The Vidarbha kingdom keeps his name. SB 9.23.38, 9.24.1

Son of Satvata, an exceedingly religious king, from whom the Bhoja kings descend. SB 9.24.7, 9.24.11

Of the Amavasu branch of the lunar line. Not Bhima the Pandava, nor Bhima of Vidarbha. VP 4.7; SB 9.15.2
